title: 1983, Structured Literacy, and Systematic Phonics Instruction
author: Andy Johnson
summary: Andy Johnson, a veteran reading educator, argues from a critical, balanced-literacy standpoint that today's structured literacy programs are largely the commercial basals of 1983 with new branding. He begins with his own first year of teaching, when he followed the teacher's manual with fidelity and sent struggling readers to lower groups. He mocks educational jar-buzz, claims the term structured literacy was coined to unify and sell what the dyslexia community does, and says structured and systematic mean only that there is a scope and sequence. He lists research claims that systematic phonics is not more effective than unsystematic or meaning-based approaches, that contextualized phonics and balanced approaches fare better, and that independent reading is essential. He objects that fidelity mandates strip teachers of professional judgement, and he advises teachers handed a basal to read it, adopt and adapt, and include authentic writing and self-selected reading. The piece is polemical and contests the mainstream science of reading consensus, and it ends with a plug for his book.
points: Johnson argues that modern commercial structured literacy programs repeat the 1983 basal model of scope-and-sequence charts, fidelity mandates and worksheets.
He claims structured literacy is a marketing term and that its structured, systematic and cumulative features simply describe a scope and sequence.
He cites studies by Bowers, Wyse and Bradbury, and Hruby to argue that systematic phonics is not demonstrably superior and that contextualized, balanced approaches are more likely to succeed.
Requiring teachers to implement programs with fidelity is appropriate for experiments but inappropriate for real classrooms with non-standardized children.
His advice to teachers given a basal is to read it, adopt and adapt it, skip or add as needed, and include authentic writing, self-selected reading and conversation about books.
quotes: So, I followed the directions in the teacher’s manual as if they were holy writ. In fact, I followed the directions with what we call “fidelity”. And because of my fidelity to the manual, I thought I was a good reading teacher.

What bothers me to this day is that I could have done so much better. I can still see the faces of the frustrated students who struggled to sound out words when they read and who couldn’t seem to put all letters in the correct order when they spelled words.
Educational jar-buzz are words and terms used in education and academia to create a façade of scholarly importance, intellectual authority, or theoretical sophistication (see Figure 1).
But all this really means is that there’s a scope and sequence. This is a list of teeny-tiny reading subskills (scope) laid out in the order in which they are to be taught (sequence).

Systematic phonics instruction is not more effective than unsystematic phonics instruction (Bowers, 2020; Camilli et al., 2006;). It is; however, significantly more boring than reading good books and learning phonics in this context.

While this may be appropriate for experimental research where control and treatment groups need to follow strict parameters in order to isolate a variable; it is neither effective nor appropriate when educating students in the uncontrolled confines of the real world.
And since real human beings are not standardized products, it would be educational malpractice to insist that teachers follow a recipe with “fidelity”.

In other words, teachers should be treated as fully competent professionals who are able to use their knowledge, expertise, and experience (just like professionals in any other field) to make decisions that are best for their students.
Don’t be afraid to skip things, add things, or teach things in ways that make sense to you.
